assessment.title: Interpreting measurement evidence
assessment.diagnostic_focus: Distinguish score consistency, measurement uncertainty, and evidence supporting a particular score interpretation.

design.section_summary: Interpret measurement statistics without treating them as definitive proof of validity or exact individual scores.

objectives.statement: Evaluate what measurement evidence does and does not support in context.
evidence_requirements: Explain why internal consistency alone does not establish validity.
Identify the need for evidence when a test is used for a new purpose.

misconception_hypotheses.statement: High reliability is sufficient to establish validity for any use.
student_language_examples: A reliable test must be valid.
misconception_hypotheses.why_plausible: Students may conflate consistency with the meaning or appropriateness of a score interpretation.

generation_settings.context_notes: Treat distractor choices as hypotheses requiring reasoning evidence, not diagnoses.

items.stem: A scale has high internal consistency in a sample. Which conclusion is best supported by that result alone?

options.label: A
options.text: The scale is valid for every intended use.

options.label: B
options.text: The item scores show consistency, but validity requires further evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: Every student's observed score is exact.

options.label: D
options.text: The scale must have the same reliability in every population.

items.target_reasoning_note: Distinguish score consistency from validity of an interpretation.
essential_elements: Internal consistency describes how consistently the items work together in this sample.
Consistency alone does not establish what the scores mean or whether a use is justified.

distractor_rationales.A: Treats high reliability as evidence that the scores are valid for any use.
distractor_rationales.C: Treats a reliable scale as giving exact individual scores, overlooking measurement error.
distractor_rationales.D: Treats reliability as a fixed property of the scale rather than of scores from a particular population.

items.stem: What does the standard error of measurement help describe?

options.label: A
options.text: Whether every item measures the intended construct.

options.label: B
options.text: The exact true score of each student.

options.label: C
options.text: Measurement uncertainty associated with a score.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether a test is appropriate for any population.

items.target_reasoning_note: Recognize that observed scores involve measurement uncertainty.
essential_elements: The SEM describes the uncertainty around an observed score.
An observed score does not reveal a student's exact true score.

distractor_rationales.A: Confuses evidence about score precision with evidence about what the items measure.
distractor_rationales.B: Treats the observed score as the exact true score.
distractor_rationales.D: Treats a precision statistic as evidence that the test suits any population.

items.stem: A test developed for course placement is proposed for professional certification. What is the most defensible next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Evaluate evidence supporting the proposed certification interpretation and use.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve the new use if internal consistency is high.

options.label: C
options.text: Assume placement evidence automatically supports certification.

options.label: D
options.text: Reject every test originally developed for a different purpose.

items.target_reasoning_note: Evaluate whether evidence is sufficient for a proposed new use.
essential_elements: A new use needs evidence for that interpretation, population and use.
Existing evidence neither transfers automatically nor rules the new use out.

distractor_rationales.B: Treats high internal consistency as enough evidence for a new use.
distractor_rationales.C: Assumes validity evidence for one use carries over to another.
distractor_rationales.D: Rejects a new use outright instead of weighing the evidence for it.
